newsitem.title: USA: Senate raises Medicare eligiibility age, means-test.
newsitem.headline: Senate raises Medicare eligiibility age, means-test.

text.p: The Senate Tuesday voted to make affluent seniors pay more for Medicare and gradually raise the eligibility age, signalling that lawmakers were ready to take politically tough steps to ensure the program's solvency.
By a 70-30 margin the Senate supported a plan making single seniors with incomes of more than $50,000 and couples making more than $75,000 pay higher premiums for Medicare doctors' coverage.

Lawmakers also voted to increase the Medicare eligibility age to 67 from the current 65. The change would be phased in slowly through 2027. Americans currently age 59 would see no increase, those now 36 and under would face a two-year delay.

The vote showed a surprising bipartisan willingness to address the long-term financing problems of Medicare after the relentless attacks Democrats waged against Republicans on the issue before the 1996 elections.
Supporters warned the changes were merely a preview of painful reforms needed to protect Medicare's long-term financial health in the next century as baby boomers retire.

"Some may have thought that there has been a leakage of reality about the social insurance programmes of the American nation, that only crisis brings us foward to sensible responses," said New York Democrat Daniel Patrick Moynihan.
"I think today we proved just the opposite," he said.
Opponents said Medicare means testing would not save much money and called the changes an alarming initiative that threatened the government's social contract with senior citizens.

"Medicare was meant to be portable, affordable and undeniable," said Maryland Democratic Sen. Barbara Mikulski. "Is Medicare meant to be affordable for senior citizens or was it meant to be affordable for government?"

The action came as the Senate debated balanced budget legislation. The House version of the budget bill, to be voted on Wednesday, does not include the changes. A battle is expected when lawmakers work out a final compromise.
Medicare Part B is voluntary, but nearly all eligible seniors choose it as it covers doctor, laboratory, outpatient hospital and other services not provided by regular Medicare.
The current monthly premium is $43.80. Seniors' monthly payment reflects only a quarter of the actual programme cost. The federal government subsidises the remaining 75 percent.

Under the legislation, the federal premium subsidy phase-out would begin at $50,000 for individuals and $75,000 for couples. Seniors in the highest income bracket would pay about $2,160 a year in premiums, up from the current $540.
Texas Republican Phil Gramm argued that without a means test, "We are going to ask moderate-income working families to subsidise people in retirement making between $100,000 to $125,000."
The change would affect about 1.5 million seniors, raising less than $4 billion over five years, sponsors said.

The higher eligibility age would be phased in through 2027. It is designed to track a 1983 reform plan that gradually raises the Social Security benefits age. Supporters said delaying eligibility was fair because life expectancy had increased since Medicare's founding.
Pennsylvania Republican Sen. Rick Santorum, 38, the youngest member of the Senate, said Americans needed to sacrifice to protect Medicare -- not just for current recipients but for his generation.
Opponents said the change would hurt blue-collar Americans who may have health problems and no private insurance.

"There's a difference between a senator ... and the worker that's out there on the line day after day after day," Iowa Democrat Tom Harkin complained. "(This) sticks it right in their back one more time."
Twelve Democrats voted to raise the eligibility age and five Democrats voted no.
The White House complained the means test and higher eligibility age were not part of the original balanced budget deal worked out with Congress.
The underlying Medicare legislation will keep the programme solvent for nearly a decade, but the long-term financial prognosis is questionable without major structural changes.
Earlier Tuesday, the Senate blocked a Democratic effort to delete a new $5 co-payment for Medicare home health visits.

The action came as the Senate debated massive legislation reducing Medicare spending by about $115 billion over five years and cutting the Medicaid programme for the poor, elderly and disabled by $13.6 billion.
